title: Donald Treadwell (Lone Otter)
summary: Donald Treadwell, also known as Lone Otter, was an Unkechaug writer, historian, healer, and community leader whose work connected Native-authored history, education, governance, and public health.
content:
Donald Treadwell (1937–1994), also known as Lone Otter, was an Unkechaug writer, historian, healer, and community leader. His life connected childhood experiences of unequal schooling, adult education, writing, tribal governance, and practical work to improve health conditions at the Poospatuck Reservation. His own writing and later historical accounts preserve both personal memory and public Unkechaug history.1

Schooling and adult education

Treadwell remembered the crowding, poverty, and social pressure that Unkechaug children encountered while traveling to and attending public school. John A. Strong quotes Treadwell’s 1988 memoir directly, allowing readers to hear his account rather than only a later historian’s summary. As an adult, Treadwell served in the military, traveled in Europe, and earned a bachelor’s degree from Empire State College at age fifty. The available source does not identify a military branch, rank, or war, so this biography does not infer them.2

Writing Unkechaug history

In 1988, Treadwell completed an unpublished memoir titled Turtle People: The Unkechaug People of Spirit Island. Strong drew on that manuscript for family and community memories, including Treadwell’s own description of school life. In 1992, writing as Lone Otter, he published My People, The Unkechaug. These works matter because they approach Unkechaug history from within the community and connect remembered experience with a broader public record.3

Leadership and a date conflict in the record

Strong records that after Chief Edwin “Red Fox” Treadwell died in April 1981, his nephew Donald Treadwell was elected chief and was respected by people across an earlier community division. A later compiled chief list by Donna Gentle Spirit Barron assigns Lone Otter the date 1991. Because the sources conflict, this article preserves both records rather than silently treating one as certain. Strong’s narrative is used for the sequence; Barron’s different list date remains part of the citation record.4

Clean water and community health

As chief, Lone Otter connected recurring illness with contaminated reservation water and worked with Brookhaven officials on a public-water project. Strong describes funding assembled through federal clean-water support and town community-development funds. By 1993, water mains had begun connecting reservation homes to a safer supply. This work placed public health, infrastructure, and the responsibilities of government at the center of tribal leadership.5

Remembering Lone Otter

Strong records that Treadwell died in 1994 and was honored with a traditional ceremony. The public map keeps the associated location broad. His legacy remains visible in Native-authored history, in the memories he preserved, and in community work that joined cultural knowledge with everyday needs.6

References

  • John A. Strong, The Unkechaug Indians of Eastern Long Island: A History (Norman: University of Oklahoma Press, 2011), pp. x, 10, 240–241, 252–253, and 259.
  • John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700 (1997), p. 280.
  • Donna Gentle Spirit Barron, The Long Island Indians and Their New England Ancestors (2008), p. 117.
  • Donald Treadwell (Lone Otter), Turtle People: The Unkechaug People of Spirit Island (unpublished memoir, 1988), cited through Strong.
  • Donald Treadwell (Lone Otter), My People, The Unkechaug (Kiva Press, 1992).
why_this_matters: Donald Treadwell’s life preserves an Unkechaug account of twentieth-century schooling, writing, tribal leadership, and the practical work of improving water and health conditions at the Poospatuck Reservation.
